provisioning: An archaeologist should check the community estimates and construction of the production index before anyone converts these curves into rice surpluses.
relocation: A regional historian should assess whether the assumed outside opportunities and movement rules describe plausible alternatives to staying at Angkor.
petri: A food-system analyst should examine storage, extraction and repair assumptions before treating the simulated growth path as a reconstruction of Angkor.
monsoon: A climate specialist and archaeologist should check the conversion from regional drought proxy to harvest and compare the decline dates with independent records.
cambodia: A Cambodian education specialist should check programme costs, migration patterns and locally measured effects before recommending any programme from these scenarios.
china: A labour economist should check demand shocks, network access and the reporting-definition change before interpreting the fitted curve as a policy diagnosis.
teachers: A ministry planner should replace the synthetic starting workforce with actual age, training and departure data before using this projection to set recruitment targets.
angkor: The grain and spending accounts need repair before a historian can use this older model to interpret population or military capacity.
campaign: A historian and provisioning specialist should check routes, mobilisation calendars, capture rates and food requirements. This engine guarantees captures after funded campaigns and has no opposing strategy.
signalling: A historian should assess audience behaviour and tribute relationships before treating the assumed stone-and-elephant weights as evidence of historical beliefs.
obligations: A historian should verify outside deliveries, recurring bills and the assumed two-year departure trigger before treating court exit as an explanation for Angkor.
mandala: This reference fails the leading-centre check. Its geography and population scale need revision before anyone uses it to explain Angkor’s political position.
credentials: A comparative education researcher should align country targets and obtain missing wealth gradients before interpreting acceptance shares as evidence favouring a theory.
institutions: These four scenarios each have one trial. More runs and explicit spending accounts are needed before assessing how reliably temple relief changes outcomes.
flight: A historian should assess migration evidence; a food-system modeller must add refuge production before this engine can support conclusions about survival outside state control.
maintenance: The timing repair is verified, but farm output still ignores the remaining workforce. Assess maintenance needs and labour dependence before interpreting the population loss historically.
accounts: The accounts balance, but rates remain hypothetical. A historian should constrain labour and food claims; military conclusions require actual campaigns and frontier supply costs.
cohort: A planner should derive flow rates from two consecutive years of enrolment and repeater data, and check repeater reporting, before reading wastage from this cohort.
sector: An education economist should replace the stylised country with national enrolment, salary and budget data before using the financing gap in a sector plan.
schoolmap: A district planner should replace the synthetic villages with mapped settlements, roads and terrain before choosing sites from this tool.
lays: An assessment specialist should check how national test results were harmonised before comparing learning-adjusted years across countries or over time.
absorption: A labour economist should check the employment elasticity and replacement rate against labour-force survey data before drawing conclusions about graduate unemployment.
